co_cactus_rose_cliff.blurb: Cactus Rose Cliff is a steep limestone wall in the Bank section of Shelf Road, up a short trail from the dirt road beyond the campground. The climbing is almost entirely bolted sport, sustained and technical on edges and pockets, with the bulk of the lines in the 5.10 to 5.12 range and a thin spread of easier ones. Tornado of Souls and Cactus Rose are among the best-known lines. Right of the main wall, short walls tucked into the trees stay shadier. Limestone here can be flaky, so test holds and wear a helmet. Shelf Road is a popular cool-season destination and fills up on winter weekends.
co_cactus_rose_cliff.parking_note: Use the day-use lot by the Bank campground and walk up the dirt road; roadside parking along the route is discouraged.
co_cactus_rose_cliff.approach: Walk the dirt road for roughly half a mile, then take the trail that heads left and switchbacks up to the base of the cliff.

_expect.name: West Ridge - part D - Xanadu to Pony Express

co_west_ridge_part_d_xanadu_to_pony_expr.blurb: This stretch of Eldorado Canyon's West Ridge is the most crack-heavy part of the sandstone band, and it is almost entirely traditional climbing, mostly single pitches from easy fifth class through the 5.11s with a few harder lines. Hand Crack and Xanadu are the standouts. The ridge faces southwest, so it catches plenty of sun and suits cooler days. Some sections hold loose rock, particularly the upper walls, so wear a helmet and treat holds with suspicion. Getting here takes real effort, and the walk-in is long enough to keep crowds thin. Most parties rappel off rather than walk down.
co_west_ridge_part_d_xanadu_to_pony_expr.approach: Several ways in exist. From the park's west end, follow the canyon trail to the Rincon turnoff, then scramble across talus and drop down to this section of the ridge. Alternatively, start at the Milton Boulder pullout and reach the base across the creek or by a new bridge. Allow well over 25 minutes.

co_new_river_wall_the.blurb: The New River Wall sits right beside Clear Creek in the canyon west of Golden, an overhanging, powerful wall that serves as the canyon's hard-sport destination. Most of the lines are bolted pitches in the 5.13 and 5.14 range, with a few trad lines and a set of boulder problems, so it is not a place for beginners. Sonic Youth is the best known of the lot. The wall stays shaded and cold through the winter, and in late spring and early summer high water can swamp the belay ledge by the river. Expect road traffic and tunnel noise nearby.
co_new_river_wall_the.parking_note: Pull into the big paved lot just before the second tunnel, the same one serving nearby Highwire Crag.

co_sunday_wall.blurb: Sunday Wall is the most visited crag in Unaweep Canyon, a big face of solid gneiss and granite on Access Fund land beside Highway 141. The climbing is mostly traditional, on cracks and thin faces up to several pitches, with a handful of bolted sport lines that are among the few in the canyon. Grades run from easy up to the low 5.13s, with the heart of it around 5.10 and 5.11. Sweet Sunday Serenade and Sun Dancer are favorites for moderate climbers, and Bridge of Air is the hard classic. At around 7,000 feet, afternoon weather can arrive quickly. Most parties rappel, though a few routes can be walked off.
co_sunday_wall.parking_note: Use the large dirt pullout on the north side of the highway, marked by an Access Fund sign.

co_piedra_river_lower_west.blurb: A small creekside cliff near Pagosa Springs, Piedra River Lower West is mostly bolted sport climbing, with a smaller number of trad lines, top ropes and a few boulder problems close to the water. Routes are concentrated between 5.8 and 5.12, with the greatest number in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, so it suits a mixed group. Mild Hops, Wild Hops and Hopstacle Course are among the better-known lines. The trail is shared with horses and hikers, so keep gear and belayers off the path. Poison ivy grows along the creek in summer, and a stick clip helps on some starts.
co_piedra_river_lower_west.approach: Park in the lot across the river, take the Ice Caves Trail downstream and bear left at the fork, then drop to the water; the first route is on your right and the wall continues along the river.

co_brown_cloud_rocks.blurb: Brown Cloud Rocks is one of the short-cliff sectors along North Table Mountain above Golden, built from dark volcanic lava rock. The routes are brief single pitches, a mix of traditional crack and dihedral climbing with some bolted lines and top ropes, mostly at moderate grades through the 5.10s. It is a handy spot for a quick session close to Denver. The cliffs face south and west, which makes them pleasant on cool, sunny days, while warm weather can leave the rock polished and slick. Rattlesnakes turn up in summer and fall. Anchors get heavy use, so lower or rappel with your own gear when you can.
co_brown_cloud_rocks.parking_note: Start from the Golden Cliffs trailhead lot, using the lower lot first and the upper one only for overflow.
co_brown_cloud_rocks.approach: Take the main trail up from the lot toward the cliff band and follow it to this sector; expect around 15 minutes of walking.

co_bierstadt_area.blurb: The Bierstadt Area is the best-known cluster of granite boulders on Mount Blue Sky, set in a wilderness cirque at roughly 11,000 feet. Problems are a mix of friendly V0 to V4 lines and bold highballs up to V10 or higher, many 15 to 25 feet tall, so pads and spotters matter. Timeline, The Ladder and Dark Crystal are common first tickets, and Bierstadt itself is the area's famous hard test. Weather turns fast at this elevation, so bring layers and rain gear. Because hikers use the same trail, keep chalk and brushing light, keep dogs leashed, and never leave pads behind.
co_bierstadt_area.parking_note: Leave the car at the Echo Lake picnic area, just west of the mile 13 marker on the byway.
co_bierstadt_area.approach: Hike the Chicago Lakes Trail over the ridge and down switchbacks, then follow it to the Bierstadt Block, a few minutes beyond a trail junction.
